coredata.dc:description: A gene encoding cutinase from Fusarium solani was cloned and overexpressed in Pichia pastoris. The recombinant cutinase with a molecular weight of 24 kDa was then purified to homogeneity. The enzyme presents degradation capacity for poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) and exhibits the optimum pH and temperature of 8.0 and 50 °C, respectively. Enzyme activity is enhanced by K+ and Na+ and inhibited by Zn2+, Fe2+, Mn2+, and Co2+. The inhibitions of different chemicals on recombinant enzyme activity were examined. EDTA and β-mercaptoethanol exert significant inhibitory effect. The degradation of PBS films in the presence of the recombinant enzyme was further studied. Results showed that enzymatic degradation is a rapid process, and the PBS films were degraded completely after approximately 6 h. The characteristics of PBS films after degradation were analyzed. With the extension of degradation time, the surfaces of PBS films became rougher and holes appeared with a gradually increasing trend. Differential scanning calorimetry and scanning electron microscopy analyses revealed that both amorphous and crystalline regions of PBS were degraded by the recombinant enzyme. Wide-angle X-ray diffractometer also indicated the crystallinity of PBS has a gradual downward trend with the extension of degradation time. Gel permeation chromatography showed the molecular weight of PBS has no obvious change before and after degradation.

head.ce:title: Enzymatic degradation of poly(butylene succinate) by cutinase cloned from Fusarium solani

ce:affiliation.ce:textfn: College of Chemistry, Chemical Engineering and Environmental Engineering, Liaoning Shihua University, Fushun, 113001, China

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A gene encoding cutinase from Fusarium solani was cloned and overexpressed in Pichia pastoris. The recombinant cutinase with a molecular weight of 24 kDa was then purified to homogeneity. The enzyme presents degradation capacity for poly(butylene succinate) (PBS) and exhibits the optimum pH and temperature of 8.0 and 50 °C, respectively. Enzyme activity is enhanced by K+ and Na+ and inhibited by Zn2+, Fe2+, Mn2+, and Co2+. The inhibitions of different chemicals on recombinant enzyme activity were examined. EDTA and β-mercaptoethanol exert significant inhibitory effect. The degradation of PBS films in the presence of the recombinant enzyme was further studied. Results showed that enzymatic degradation is a rapid process, and the PBS films were degraded completely after approximately 6 h. The characteristics of PBS films after degradation were analyzed. With the extension of degradation time, the surfaces of PBS films became rougher and holes appeared with a gradually increasing trend. Differential scanning calorimetry and scanning electron microscopy analyses revealed that both amorphous and crystalline regions of PBS were degraded by the recombinant enzyme. Wide-angle X-ray diffractometer also indicated the crystallinity of PBS has a gradual downward trend with the extension of degradation time. Gel permeation chromatography showed the molecular weight of PBS has no obvious change before and after degradation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Introduction
ce:section.ce:para: The uncontrolled use and disposal of non-degradable synthetic polymers, which are typically petroleum-based polymers, increase environmental burden on solid waste management and waste non-renewable petroleum resources [1]. To reduce the environmental impact of synthetic plastics, some industries have started to produce biodegradable plastics, aliphatic polyester in general, as a substitute. Many different kinds of biodegradable aliphatic plastics are produced, including polyglycolide, polylactic acid (PLA), polycaprolactone (PCL), poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), and polyhydroxyalkanoates [2].

PBS, which was invented in the early 1990s by Showa Highpolymer in Japan, is one of the most promising biodegradable aliphatic polyesters [3]. Since then, the crystal structure, crystallization, and melting behavior of PBS have been further investigated [4–8]. Several works evaluated PBS degradability in PBS-degrading microorganisms [9–11]. Several PBS depolymerase genes have also been cloned and expressed. Uchida et al. [12] cloned a gene encoding PBS depolymerase from Acidovorax delafieldii strain BS-3. The clone expressed in Escherichia coli can degrade both PBS and poly[(tetramethylene succinate)-co-adipate]. Akutsu-Shigeno et al. [13] cloned a gene encoding PLA depolymerase from Paenibacillus amylolyticus strain TB-13; the gene was overexpressed in E. coli, and the purified recombinant PLA depolymerase, which was identified as lipase, also exhibited degradation activity toward PBS.

In our previous studies [15], a PBS-degrading strain Fusarium sp. FS1301 was isolated and found to exhibit high degradability of PBS. PBS depolymerase was purified and analyzed by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry. The deduced amino acid sequence showed 100% similarity to cutinase (NCBI Accession Number: Q99174.1) from Fusarium solani.

Recently, the use of the methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris as a host for the expression of recombinant proteins has become increasingly attractive. In addition to the appropriate post-translational modifications for protein functionality, P. pastoris often allows the recombinant protein to be secreted in large quantities. In this work, the cutinase gene from F. solani, which exhibits PBS degradability, was cloned and overexpressed in P. pastoris. The degradation behavior of the recombinant enzyme was characterized by analyzing PBS films before and after degradation. Specifically, PBS degradation rate was calculated, and the degraded PBS films were characterized.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Materials and methods
Chemicals and cultivation medium
ce:section.ce:para: PBS was obtained from Anqing He Xing Chemical Corp. Ltd. (Anqing, China). The number-average molecular weight (Mn) of PBS was 150 000 to 210 000. Poly (butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA) with a Mn 140 000 to 150 000 were obtained from Showa Highpolymer (Tokyo, Japan). Poly(l-lactic acid) (PLA) with a Mn of 400,000 were kindly supplied by Zhejiang Hisun Biomaterial Co. (Taizhou, China). Poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) with a melt index of 5 g/10 min and reported a viscosity-average molecular weight of 70000 were supplied by Solvay (Brussels, Belgium). The yeast strain P. pastoris X33 and the expression vector pPICZα were purchased from Invitrogen. Restriction endonucleases, T4 DNA ligase, and agarose gel DNA purification kit were obtained from Takara Bio (Dalian) Inc. (Dalian, China). Yeast nitrogen base and biotin were obtained from Beijing Dingguo Changsheng Biotechnology Co. Ltd. (Beijing, China). p-nitrophenyl butyrate (pNPB) was obtained from Sigma. Unless otherwise stated, all the other chemicals used were of analytical grade. Yeast extract peptone dextrose medium (YPD), buffered glycerol–complex media (BMGY), and buffered methanol complex media (BMMY) were prepared as described in the Invitrogen Pichia expression kit.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Gene synthesis and recombinant vector construction
ce:section.ce:para: According to the codon of P. pastoris yeast, the gene sequence of the cutinase (NCBI accession number: gi|2493916) from F. solani was redesigned without altering the amino acid sequence and named as FSC. The rearranged gene sequence FSC was synthesized by Shanghai Sangon Biological Engineering Technology and Services Co., Ltd. (Sangon, Shanghai, China). The FSC gene fragment and the plasmid pPICZα were digested with EcoR I and Not I and then ligated. The right transformants were verified by endonuclease digestion and agarose gel electrophoresis. Finally, a recombinant plasmid called pPICZα-FSC was obtained.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Transformation of P. pastoris and induced expression of FSC
ce:section.ce:para: The reconstructed vector pPICZα-FSC was linearized by SacI digestion, and then the purified DNA fragment containing the FSC gene was transformed into P. pastoris X33 competent cells by electroporation. Yeast transformants were screened and selected on YPD containing different concentrations of zeocin. The chosen positive transformants were cultured in BMGY at 30 °C and 220 rpm until the OD600 reached 4.5. Yeast cells were harvested and resuspended in BMMY and cultured for 72 h (29 °C, 220 rpm) to induce protein expression. The expression culture (600 μL) was centrifuged at 4 °C and 12,000 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatant was placed in TCA Protein Precipitation Kit (Sangon, China) to precipitate protein for SDS–PAGE and WB assay.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Protein purification and PBS depolymerase activity assay
ce:section.ce:para: The selected high expression strain was cultured for 72 h (29 °C, 220 rpm) in BMMY to induce protein expression. The expression culture was centrifuged at 4 °C and 12,000 rpm for 15 min. The supernatant was loaded onto a High-Affinity Ni-NTA Resin (GenScript, Nanjing, China). The fractions with PBS degradation activity were combined and dialyzed with distilled deionized water. The purified recombined enzyme was collected after lyophilization.

PBS depolymerase activity was assayed as follows: 1 mL of the enzyme solution was added to 3 mL of PBS emulsion and incubated at 40 °C for 20 min. An ultraviolet spectrophotometer (2600 UV-VIS; UNICO, USA) was used to test the optical density (OD630 nm) before and after incubation. One unit of PBS-degrading enzyme activity was defined as a 0.001 OD decrease in the absorbance per minute at 630 nm [16].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of pH and temperature on the PBS degradation activity of the recombinant enzyme

ce:list-item.ce:para: Optimal pH and temperature: The optimal pH of the recombinant enzyme was 4.0–10.0 at different pH levels. The optimal temperature of the enzyme ranged from 30 °C to 70 °C.
Stability of enzyme activity at different pH levels: The recombinant enzyme was incubated at different pH levels (4.0–10.0) for 24 h at 37 °C. Enzyme activity was tested under standard conditions.
Thermostability of the enzyme: The recombinant enzyme was dissolved in potassium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) and stored at 20 °C–80 °C for 1 h.

ce:section.ce:para: Residual activity was tested under standard conditions. The standard conditions were described in Section 2.4. The activity of the recombinant enzyme assayed under standard conditions was considered as 100%.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of metal ions and chemicals
ce:section.ce:para: Different metal ions (Na+, K+, Mg2+, Ni2+, Fe2+, Co2+, Mn2+, and Zn2+) and chemicals [methanol, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), β-mercaptoethanol, phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), and Tween 20] were added into the PBS emulsion. The activity of the recombinant enzyme after the addition of metal ions and chemicals was then tested. The activity of the recombinant enzyme assayed under standard conditions was considered as 100%.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PBS films by the recombinant enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: The Biotech RC Dialysis Tubing (3.5–5.0 kDa, Spectrum Laboratories, Inc., USA) including 10 mL of 20 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) containing 20 μg/mL recombinant enzyme and PBS films (30 mm × 10 mm × 0.1 mm) were incubated in 20 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) at 40 °C. After incubation for different durations, the films were carefully collected, thoroughly washed with deionized water, and vacuum-dried at 50 °C until a constant weight was obtained. The surface of pre- and post-degraded PBS films was observed under a scanning electron microscope (XL30 ESEM FEG; FEI Co., Netherlands) at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Activities of the recombinant enzyme for various substrates
ce:section.ce:para: The recombinant enzyme was transferred into PLA emulsion (0.1%, w/v), PBSA emulsion (0.1%, w/v), and PCL emulsion (0.1%, w/v). The assay of activity of the recombinant enzyme for PLA, PBSA, and PCL was described in Section 2.4.

pNPB was also used as substrate for assay the esterase activity of the recombinant enzyme. The assay was measured in a final volume of 1 mL containing pNPB (1 mM), the enzyme, and the buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 10 mM NaCl, and 50 mM sodium taurodeoxycholate, pH 8.0) at 20 °C. The reaction was initiated by the addition of pNPB. The hydrolysis of pNPB was spectrophotometrically monitored for the formation of the p-nitrophenol at 405 nm. One unit of enzyme activity is defined as the production of 1 μmol of p-nitrophenol per minute [17].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Kinetic characterization of the recombinant enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: pNPB was used as substrate for the kinetic study of the recombinant enzyme. The assays were performed using 50 μg/mL enzyme with at least five concentrations of pNPB at pH 8.0 and 37 °C. The kinetic constant, Km, was determined from a Lineweaver-Burk plot [18].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of PBS films degraded by the recombinant enzyme
ce:section.ce:para: The thermal behavior of the pre- and post-degraded films was investigated using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA; Pyris-1, Perkin-Elmer, Waltham, MA, USA). All scans were conducted from 100 °C to 600 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 under nitrogen atmosphere. The thermal properties of the samples were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC; Diamond, Perkin–Elmer USA). The pre- and post-degraded films were tested by heating from 50 °C to 230 °C at a rate of 10 °C min−1 under nitrogen atmosphere. The crystalline structures of the films were assayed by wide-angle X-ray diffractometer (WXRD, PW1700, Philips, Holland) equipped with a Ni-filtered Cu Kα radiation source. Measurements were performed at 40 kV, 200 mA, and scan angles ranging from 5° to 50° at a scan rate of 5° min−1.

The pre- and post-degraded films were also analyzed by Gel Permeation Chromatography (GPC). GPC measurements were performed at room temperature using the Agilent 1200 system and Agilent ChemStation software (Agilent Technologies, USA) to keep and reproduce the results. An Agilent 1200 refractive index detector was used at working temperature of 35 °C, with a temperature controller and tungsten lamp. Chloroform was used as eluent at a flow rate of 0.80 mL/min with a stabilization pressure of 35 bar and a sample concentration of 1.5 mg/mL. A Waters Styragel HT column (Waters Corporation, Milford, USA) was used and different molecular masses polystyrene as standard.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Results
Gene cloning and vector reconstruction
ce:section.ce:para: The FSC gene (approximately 711 bps) amplified by PCR was inserted into pPICZα to reconstruct the recombinant vector, which was named as pPICZα–FSC (Fig. 1 ). Endonuclease digestion and agarose gel electrophoresis were used to screen the reconstructed plasmid. Result of sequencing with 5′/3′ AOX1 primers showed that the integrated gene was identical to the reported gene sequence of cutinase isolated from F. solani.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Induced recombinant expression of FSC and purification of FSC
ce:section.ce:para: After reconstruction, the recombinant vector FSC was introduced into P. pastoris by electrotransformation. The correct recombinant yeast transformants were then cultured for expression of FSC, and the dialyzed supernatant was assayed by SDS–PAGE and WB. The yeast transformant with highest protein expression level and PBS depolymerase activity and was thus selected for subsequent purification. The homogeneity of the purified protein was verified by SDS–PAGE. The results showed a single band corresponding to purified FSC with a molecular weight of 24 kDa (Fig. 2 ).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of temperature and pH on PBS degradation by FSC
ce:section.ce:para: The effect of pH on the PBS-degrading activity of FSC was assayed under standard conditions except for pH (pH 4.0 to 10). In the pH range of 4.5–8.0, the PBS-degrading activity increased with increasing pH and reached the maximal value at pH 8.0. In contrast, no enzyme activity was detected under acidic conditions (pH ≤ 4.5) (Fig. 3 a). The PBS-degrading activity of FSC was also assayed under standard conditions except for temperatures of 30–70 °C. The maximal activity of the enzyme was observed at 50 °C (Fig. 3b).

FSC was incubated at pHs of 4–10 at 37 °C for 24 h, followed by an assay for residual activity under the standard conditions to confirm the stability at various pHs. As shown in Fig. 3c, FSC was quite stable in the whole pH test range. FSC was incubated at various temperatures between 20 and 80 °C for 1 h, and residual activity was assayed to confirm the stability at various temperatures. The PBS degrading activity of FSC was decreased upon exposure to increasing temperature from 20 to 80 °C and was abolished at 0.80 °C. FSC exhibited a relative high activity from 20 °C to 50 °C, and the PBS degradation activity remained at 50% at 50 °C (Fig. 3d).

According to the assay on the effects of temperature and pH on PBS degradation by FSC (Fig. 3a and b), the optimal temperature and pH for FSC on PBS degradation were 50 °C and 8.0, respectively. The effect of pH stability on the recombinant enzyme FSC maintained relative high activity on PBS degradation from pH 4.0 to 10.0 (Fig. 3c). (Fig. 3d).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of various metal irons and chemicals on PBS degradation by FSC
ce:section.ce:para: Table 1 shows that the effects of various metal ions on PBS degradation by FSC. Most metal ions exerted no significant effect at 1 mM. However, Zn2+ and Co2+ markedly inhibited enzyme activity at this concentration. When the metal ion concentration was increased to 10 mM, Na+ and K+ showed considerably increased capability on the activity of FSC and the activity of FSC effect by Zn2+ and Co2+ was further decreased. The effect of 10 mM Fe2+ and Mn2+ also decreased the activity of FSC on PBS degradation.

The purified enzyme was sensitive to most assayed chemicals (Table 2 ). Evident activity loss was detected even at low concentrations [1% (v/v) or 1 mM], except for methanol, which did not affect the activity. EDTA inhibited the PBS-degrading activity of FSC, suggesting that the enzyme exhibited metal ion dependence at its active site. PMSF partly inhibited the PBS-degrading activity of FSC, indicating that a serine residue was involved in the active side of FSC. β-Mercaptoethanol inhibited the PBS-degrading activity of FSC because the compound breaks the disulfide bonds in FSC and markedly decreases the activity of the enzyme. Tween 20 also exhibits certain inhibition on PBS-degrading activity of FSC, thereby suggesting that FSC may contain hydrophobic groups at its active site.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Substrate specificity of FSC
ce:section.ce:para: The specific activities for PCL, PBSA, and PLA were assayed by the same methods with PBS and the results were shown in Fig. 4 . As shown in Fig. 4, FSC also has a nice degraded activity for PBSA (179.6 U/mg) and PCL (84.6 U/mg) besides PBS (102.4 U/mg). However, FSC has a very low degraded activity to PLA (7.6 U/mg). pNPB was used as substrate for assay the esterase activity of FSC. The specific activity of pNPB was assayed as 287 U/mg.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Kinetic characterization of FSC
ce:section.ce:para: In order to establish the relationship between the substrate and the activity of the FSC. pNPB, a normal esterase substrate, was chosen for the kinetic study of FSC. The kinetic constant Km (1.37 mM) was calculated by a Lineweaver-Burk plot (Fig. 5 ).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Degradation of PBS films by FSC
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 6 shows the weight loss of PBS films with prolonged incubation in the presence of FSC. Enzyme degradation is a fast and swift process, and PBS films were degraded completely after approximately 6 h. The weight loss profile showed two conspicuous steps (stages). Rapid weight loss occurred in the first stage (0 h–2 h), and more than 60% of the PBS film was degraded. In the second stage (2 h–6 h), the degradation slowed down and retained at high rates. The remaining 40% of PBS films was degraded completed within 4 h.

ce:section.ce:section-title: SEM of PBS films degraded by FSC
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 4 shows the surface morphology of the degraded PBS films by FSC.

The PBS films before degradation present a smooth surface (Fig. 7 a). In the initial stages of degradation (Fig. 7b), FSC eroded the surface of PBS films and some crackle formation appeared on the surface. Fig. 7c shows erosion. Several areas were already eroded, and other areas maintained a smooth appearance. The surface eroded completely and began to exhibit several small holes with prolonged degradation (Fig. 7d and e). With increasing degradation time, the surface of PBS films became rougher and the hole showed a gradual increasing trend (Fig. 7f–h).

ce:section.ce:section-title: DSC of PBS films degraded by FSC
ce:section.ce:para: The thermal properties of PBS films degraded by FSC were investigated using DSC analysis (Fig. 8 a). The melting point of pure PBS was approximately 103 °C. After being degraded by FSC, the PBS melting point did not significantly change. The crystallinity of the PBS films was calculated based on the theoretical ΔH° values of PBS (110.5 J g−1) [19]. The crystallinity decreased from 65.28% to 58.28% with prolonged degradation time (Fig. 8b). The results indicated that FSC degraded both the amorphous and crystalline regions of PBS, causing damage to the crystalline structure.

ce:section.ce:section-title: TGA of PBS films degraded by FSC
ce:section.ce:para: Changes in the thermal stability of PBS films degraded by FSC were assayed using TGA. The TGA results (Fig. 9 ) showed that decomposition temperature decreased with prolonged degradation. This finding suggests that the polymer chains of PBS were damaged by FSC.

ce:section.ce:section-title: WXRD of PBS films degraded by FSC
ce:section.ce:para: Fig. 10 shows the WAXD of the pre- and post-degraded PBS films, which indicates that the samples have the same crystal structure. The enzymatic degradation of PBS does not affect the position of the diffraction peaks. Three main characteristic diffraction peaks of PBS located at 19.4°, 21.9°, and 22.6° are assignable to (020), (021) and (110) planes of PBS, respectively [20]. Along with the increase of degradation time, the diffraction peaks area of PBS shows a declining trend. It indicated the crystallinity of PBS has a gradual downward trend with the extension of degradation time.

ce:section.ce:section-title: GPC of PBS films degraded by FSC
ce:section.ce:para: GPC of the PBS films degraded by FSC for specific time was performed and the detailed data of Mw, Mn and Mw/Mn were summarized in Table 3 . The results showed the molecular weight had almost no change before and after FSC degradation and the Mw/Mn had a little decrease trends along with the degradation time.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Discussion
ce:section.ce:para: In this work, a gene encoding cutinase, which exhibits PBD-degradation activity, from F. solani was cloned and overexpressed in P. pastoris. The recombinant enzyme FSC was purified and characterized. Compared with the enzyme purified from the zymotic fluid of Fusarium sp. FS1301 [15], the molecular mass of the recombinant enzyme FSC is slightly higher because of the added His-tag. The molecular weight of FSC and the most commonly reported PBS-degrading enzyme were all between 20 and 25 kDa [19,21,22]. Notably, PBS depolymerase activity of FSC showed improvement (recombinant enzyme, 102.4 U/mg; native enzyme purified form Fusarium sp. FS1301, 71.8 U/mg) and may be directly related to the high purity of the recombinant enzyme. The PBS depolymerase, which has been rarely reported, presented specific enzyme activity. The specific activity of the PBS-degrading enzyme, which was identified as cutinase from Aspergillus oryzae, was determined as 0.42 U/mg [21]. Although the value of the enzyme activity is lower than FSC, the enzyme activity is actually higher. It is because that the enzyme activity was defined using different calculated method. PLA depolymerase from Paenibacillus amylolyticus, which was expressed in Escherichia coli, has PBS degraded activity [13]. Because it used a different method for determination of enzyme activity, it cannot compare the enzyme activity with FSC. The optimum pH of FSC is lower than that of PBS depolymerases but remained in the alkaline range, and the optimum temperature is similar to that of the reported PBS depolymerases [13,19,22]. Analysis of substrate specificity revealed that besides PBS, FSC also has a good degraded activity for PCL and PBSA, but PLA degraded activity is very low. It is similar with the property of the enzyme from A. oryzae [21]. In fact, the native PBS depolymerase purified form F. solani was not shown a PLA degraded activity in our previous work [15]. It also may be due to the high purity of the recombinant enzyme. On the other hand, it has been reported that the cutinase from F. solani could degrade PCL [23]. Our results further validate it. The esterase activity of FSC is lower than that of the enzyme from A. oryzae which also has PBS degraded activity [21], but it is higher than that of cutinase type polyesterases from Thermobifida alba HK119 [24]. The kinetic characterization of FSC showed FSC has similar kinetic constants with cutinase from F. solani [25]. While the Km of FSC for pNPB is higher than that of enzyme from A. oryzae [21,25]. It means that the substrate affinity of FSC for pNPB is lower than that of enzyme from A. oryzae.

In this work, the degradation of PBS films by the recombinant enzyme FSC was studied. FSC showed an outstanding PBS degradation activity, and the weight loss of the PBS films was almost 100% (w/w) within 6 h of degradation. The degradation efficiency was considerably improved compared with the microbial degradation of PBS. In our previous study, Fusarium sp. FS1301 presented 80% (w/w) weight loss of PBS films after 21 days of degradation [15] and Pseudozyma antarctica resulted in 60% (w/w) weight loss within 6 weeks [26]. Maeda et al. [21] also degraded PBS and PBSA films by the cutinase purified from A. oryzae. The result showed the cutinase from A. oryzae with 80 μg/mL concentration can dissolved completely a 50 μm thick PBSA film in only 6 h. It also can degrade PBS films, but there has no accurate data on the PBS films degradation. During degradation, the PBS film was seriously damaged and exhibited difficulty in maintaining a perfect shape. This finding differs from microbial degradation; therefore, degradation rate cannot be calculated. The results of SEM also showed that the micro-structural change of films vary with microbial degradation. In our previous work on Fusarium sp. FS1301-degraded PBS films, SEM results showed that shallow holes appeared on the PBS films [15]. The surfaces of the PBS films after 3 h of degradation by FSC began to show deep holes; with prolonged degradation, the hole showed a gradual increasing trend. The filaments of Fusarium sp. FS1301 stretched into films and secreted degraded enzymes because of the degradation of PBS films. The degradation rate of the purified enzyme varied, and the PBS films directly contacted degrading enzymes rapidly. Shinozaki et al. [14] assumed that the enzymes must be in close proximity to its substrate for a specific period of time to allow efficient activity against the substrate. Direct enzymatic degradation shortens this time. The enzymes can more easily come in contact with water–soluble substrates compared with insoluble substrates. However, plastic films possess extremely low contact efficacy with enzyme molecules and possess certain properties that enable them to be adsorbed onto the surface of substrates; these properties allow the enzymes to be in close proximity to its substrate to facilitate degradation.

The crystallinity of polymer films will be increased because non-crystalline regions are degraded first, followed by the crystalline part, with increasing degradation time [27]. In the present work, DSC results showed that PBS crystallinity decreased with prolonged degradation. Hence, FSC degraded both the amorphous and crystalline regions of PBS and damaged the crystalline structure. This result is directly related to enzyme degradation within a short duration. The results of XRD also showed that the crystallinity of polymer films has a downward trend along with the increasing of degradation time. TGA results showed that the weight loss transition temperature shifted from the higher to lower with respect to degradation time. The temperature shift was due to the disintegration of the polymer chain as degradation progressed. The chain scission caused the overall molecular weight of the polymer to decrease, resulting in a broad molecular weight distribution. This molecular weight distribution caused further decrease in the degradation temperature. This finding is similar to changes in PCL [28] or PHB [29] biodegradation. GPC analyses revealed the FSC enzymatic degradation produced no change in the molecular weight of PBS. It can be explained that it has no accumulation of the low-molecular weight enzymatic degraded components, and the degradation of PBS films by FSC only happen on the surface of the films by enzyme erosion. The results are similar with those of Ju et al. [30]. Ju et al. applied lipase from Pseudomonas mendocina and proteinase K to enzymatic hydrolysis PLA and poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-4-hydroxybutyrate) (P34HB) blends and it has also no obvious change for molecular weight. While the result of Alejandra et al. [31] showed there has a correlation between the enzymatic reaction time and the molecular mass of P34HB. The molecular weight of polymer decreased along with the degradation time. This distinction should be affiliated with the different mechanisms of enzyme.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Conclusion
ce:section.ce:para: In this work, a gene encoding cutinase from F. solani was cloned and overexpressed in Pichia pastoris. The recombinant cutinase FSC showed significant PBS degradation activity. PBS film degradation must be investigated to elucidate the degradation mechanisms of this polymer PBS and use to develop technique for degradation of polymer wastes. Notably, the molecular structure of PBS shows no similarity to cutin; therefore, the specific degradation mechanism of the recombinant cutinase FSC for PBS must be further studied.

Further analysis of the higher structure of FSC will help to clarify its underlying mechanism. These works are in progress in our laboratory. Therefore, further characterization and applications of FSC in biodegradation of plastic materials are expected.
